opus-5.5.text:
I think it's going to change both the texture of daily mathematical work and, more deeply, what we consider the "interesting" part of mathematics.

Start with the daily work. A huge fraction of a working mathematician's time goes into things that aren't the creative core: checking a lemma you're fairly sure is true, chasing down whether someone in 1987 already proved the special case you need, grinding through a messy computation, or verifying that a long argument doesn't have a gap on page forty. AI systems, especially when paired with formal verification in languages like Lean, are getting very good at exactly this kind of work. So I think mathematicians will start to treat AI almost like a tireless collaborator, a very strong graduate student who never sleeps and never gets bored of case analysis.

The formal verification part matters a lot to me. Mathematics has always rested on trust. You trust the referee, you trust the community, and for really long proofs sometimes that trust is stretched thin. If AI can help translate informal proofs into machine-checkable ones, we get a kind of certainty that has never been available at scale. That changes the social structure of math: you could build on someone's result with much more confidence, and much faster.

The deeper change is about taste and direction. When verification and routine proving become cheap, the scarce resource becomes knowing which questions are worth asking. Which conjecture is beautiful? Which definition is the right one? What connection between two fields is actually illuminating, not just true? I think human mathematicians will move up a level of abstraction, becoming more like architects and less like bricklayers. That's not a demotion. It's what the best mathematicians have always done; they'll just get to spend more of their time doing it.

I also think it opens the door to a different kind of exploration. Right now you're limited by how many ideas you can personally test. If you can say, "Let's try fifty variations of this approach overnight and see which ones survive," the experimental side of mathematics becomes much richer. Mathematics could start to feel a bit more like a lab science in that respect.

There are open questions, of course. How do we train young mathematicians if the struggle of working through proofs by hand is what builds intuition? I don't think we should skip that struggle. Understanding still has to live in a human mind for mathematics to mean something to us. But I'm optimistic. Every time we've gotten a powerful new tool, from computers to computer algebra systems, mathematics hasn't shrunk. It has gotten bigger and stranger and more ambitious. I expect AI to do that on a scale we haven't seen before.

r001.rationale: The candidate says mathematicians will “move up a level of abstraction,” becoming more like architects.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare AI’s effect on mathematics to programming’s progression toward higher-level interfaces.

r003.rationale: The candidate identifies deciding “which questions are worth asking” as the scarce human role when routine proving becomes cheap.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the honest answer is that it's already changing, and it's changing in a way that's less dramatic than the headlines and more profound than most people expect.

Let me start with what I actually see day to day. Mathematicians have always divided their time between two kinds of work. There's the part where you're searching: you have a hunch, you try examples, you try to prove a lemma and it fails, you try a variant, you go read a paper from 1987 that someone mentioned at tea. And then there's the part where you're understanding: you finally see why something is true, and the whole picture reorganizes in your head. The first part is laborious and the second part is what people become mathematicians for.

What AI is doing right now is compressing the first part. A system can try a hundred approaches to a lemma overnight. It can formalize a proof in Lean and tell you, with no ambiguity, that step seven doesn't actually follow. It can read the literature more completely than any human and tell you that your "new" idea appeared in a Russian journal decades ago. None of that is the romantic part of mathematics, but it's maybe eighty percent of the hours.

So the first change is simply that the ratio shifts. Mathematicians will spend more of their time asking questions and less of it grinding. And I think this makes taste much more important. When search is cheap, the scarce thing is knowing what's worth searching for. Which conjecture is deep rather than merely hard? Which definition is the right one? That's a very human skill, and it's going to be rewarded more, not less.

The second change is about verification, and I think this one is underrated. Mathematics has a reputation for certainty, but the actual practice has a lot of "the experts believe this is fine." There are results in the literature that everyone cites and no one has fully checked. Formal proof assistants plus AI make it realistic to actually verify things at scale. That changes the social structure of the field. A graduate student who can produce a verified proof doesn't need the authority of a famous name behind them. I find that genuinely exciting.

The third change is more speculative. When AI systems start proposing conjectures and not just proving them, mathematicians will have to develop a new kind of collaboration. It's a little like what happened when computers enabled experimental mathematics: people learned to look at data, see patterns, and then ask why. I think we'll see a lot more of that, where the machine says "these two things seem to be related" and the human's job is to find the reason.

What I don't think happens is that mathematicians become obsolete. Partly because the hard questions are, almost by definition, the ones where we don't know what we're looking for yet. But mostly because mathematics isn't really a production process whose output is theorems. It's a way of understanding. A proof that no human understands is a strange object. It might be true, and that's useful, but the field will still want someone to explain why it's true, and that act of explanation is where the next question comes from.

So if I had to summarize: I think AI makes mathematicians more like mathematicians. Less time being a search engine and a proof checker, more time doing the thing only a person can do, which is deciding what matters and understanding why.

r001.rationale: The response says mathematicians will spend more time asking questions and understanding, but it does not say their reasoning will move to higher levels of abstraction.

r002.rationale: It compares AI-enabled conjecture work to experimental mathematics, but makes no comparison to programming's progression toward higher-level interfaces.

r003.rationale: It identifies human taste in choosing what to search for, asking which conjectures are deep, and deciding what matters.

astra-6.text:
I think AI could change both how we explore mathematics and how we check our work. When you’re working on a problem, you often spend a lot of time trying examples, looking for a useful formulation, or figuring out whether an approach fails for a simple reason. An AI that helps with those steps could let mathematicians explore more possibilities and get feedback much faster.

But finding a proof is only part of mathematics. We also want to understand why something is true, how it connects to other ideas, and whether it leads to an interesting new question. Even if an AI gives you a correct proof, there’s still a lot of intellectual work in turning that proof into understanding.

I’m especially interested in the interaction between creative exploration and rigorous verification. You could imagine AI suggesting an unexpected argument, and formal tools helping check each step. That would give us more room to be adventurous without treating a plausible-looking argument as established truth.

Over time, I think that could shift what mathematicians spend their attention on: more time choosing questions, developing concepts, and interpreting results. And perhaps the most exciting possibility is that AI will suggest ways of thinking that we wouldn’t have arrived at ourselves.

r001.rationale: The response says mathematicians may spend more time developing concepts and interpreting results, but it does not state that AI will lead them to reason at higher levels of abstraction.

r002.rationale: It does not compare AI’s effect on mathematics with programming’s progression toward higher-level interfaces.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says mathematicians may spend more time choosing questions, which communicates the human role of selecting what to explore.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AI could change both the pace of mathematical work and the kinds of questions we spend our time on. A lot of research involves trying examples, checking whether an argument really works, and exploring approaches that may lead nowhere. If AI can help with those steps, mathematicians could get feedback much more quickly and spend more time thinking about the underlying structure.

But finding a proof and understanding a proof are different things. You might have a correct argument and still want to know: Why is this true? What is the right way to see it? How does it connect to something else? Even as AI becomes better at producing proofs, those questions will remain important.

I’m especially interested in the possibility that AI could suggest connections we wouldn’t naturally look for. That could expand our intuition. Of course, we’ll need ways to verify its suggestions carefully, because a plausible-looking argument isn’t enough in mathematics.

So I imagine a more interactive way of working: you propose an idea, the AI helps you explore it, and what you learn changes your next question. The exciting possibility is that this helps us ask better questions, as well as answer existing ones.

r001.rationale: The response says AI could free mathematicians to think more about underlying structure, but it does not clearly say their reasoning will move to higher levels of abstraction.

r002.rationale: The response makes no comparison to programming or to the progression toward higher-level interfaces.

r003.rationale: It mentions asking better questions, but does not identify choosing which mathematical problems are worth exploring as a human role.
